Canadian Camping 


THE 

VICE-PRESIDENT’S 

PAGE 

“Chief, the water is ofT in the senior 
section.” 

“Chief, the meat hasn’t arrived yet 
ind we need it for supper.” 

“Chief, tlie tile bed is breaking out 
again.” 

“Chief, we need more craft supplies 
for the all-day programme on Tues¬ 
day.” 

“Chief, the motorboat is out of com¬ 
mission again and the milk is at the 
landing.” 

“Chief, Harry just phoned in, the 
camp truck has broken down near the 
Park gate.” 

In recent issues of the magazine we 
have had some interesting articlas writ¬ 
ten entitled. Why I Direct a Camp. 
None of them mentioned tile beds, solv¬ 
ing plumbing problems, food deliveries, 
and the hundred other minor crises that 
the camp director faces daily. When a 
camp director gets out of bed in the 
morning he knows that he will have to 
face many problems. He has no idea 
what they will be, but he can be sure 
that a number of things will crop up 
every day. 

Camp directors become camp direc¬ 
tors because they enjoy camping and 
working with people, particularly child¬ 
ren. However, in conversation with 
other camp directors, I find that most 
are concerned by the fact that the 
demands of plumlDing and logistics are 
taking them further and further away 
from the campers. 

The camp director climbs out of bed 
in the morning full of hopes and aims 
for the day, but all too often he soon 
finds himself bogged down in the mun- 


LET’S GET BACK TO THE 
CAMPERS 

by Barry G. Lowes, 

Vice President CCA, Ontario 
Director, Camp Timberlane. 

dane, the routine and the technical 
aspects of camping. He loses touch 
with the campers in the morass of 
minor crises through which he must 
slog each day. 

There is no denying that these crises 
are real and immediate: “no meat, no 
eat”, a backed-up tile bed, a broken 
motor, these are things that can’t wait. 
So Johnny has to wait. The camp will 
not stop if Johnny is put ofT until the 
water is put on. I submit that the 
camp world may not stop but Johnny’s 
may. Johnny’s problem is just as urg¬ 
ent, just as immediate and just as criti¬ 
cal as the others. It just isn’t so 
obvious. 

Camp directors seem to be with¬ 
drawing unwittingly, or are being 
forced further and further away from 
the campers. The bigger the camp, the 
.sooner this happens and the more often 
it happens. 

Isn’t it time that we, as camp direc¬ 
tors, cried “Whoa”? Isn’t it time that 
we threw ofT this yoke and broke out of 
this mud-hole of chores, these .small 
cancers that gnaw away at our time? 
Isn’t it time that we took an honest 
look at how we spend our time and 
why we are directing camps? 

Isn’t it true that the director prob¬ 
ably knows and understands the child¬ 
ren at his camp better than anyone 
else? Isn’t it true that he has probably 
had more experience than any other 
stair member at working with people? 
And yet, he delegates these most im¬ 
portant roles to assistants. These in¬ 
ternes apply the band-aids, the salve, 
turn to page 115 


Toronto, Canada, April 1963 


85 




CAMPING 


EDUCATION FOR LIFE 

by Lome E. Brown 
Co-Director, Camp Deka, B.C. 


This article is based on the opening 
address given at The Canadian Camj)- 
ing Association Annual Meeting and 
Sixth Annual Camp Directors’ Seminar 
sponsored by The Alberta Camping 
Association. 


Your Committee has suggested that 
we deal with “Programme” and “Pro¬ 
gramme Typing” in this session. 1 
should like first to explore what is pre¬ 
requisite and basic to programme: our 
philosophy of camping. If all of us 
take nothing more from this Seminar 
than the strong determination to return 
to our individual camps and evaluate 
our programme objectively in tenns of 
some of the basic issues to be raised 
here, then it will be well justified. 

If we examine the current scene as 
shown by our western society, we find 
that automation and electronics hav^e 
taken over more and more of man’s 
work, and with it many of those activi¬ 
ties that make his life purposeful. There 
has been a mass exodus from rural to 
city settings. This has created prob¬ 
lems—the affluent society, crowding, 
pressures to conformity, disintegration 
of family life, world tensions, etc. Then 
there are the great mass media of today, 
u.sing all the resources of modern psy¬ 
chology to influence man’s behaviour 
at an ever-increasing rate. 

Grattan O’Leary, our Canadian jour¬ 
nalist, observes that “We have today all 
facts and no knowledge; all specializa¬ 
tion and no wisdom; all know how and 
no know why; all signposts and no des¬ 
tination”. 'riiese are strong words. 


Many of us regret the lack of values 
among young people, those sources of 
strength that could help them in their 
personal development. Someone has 
suggested that these values include new 
experience, recognition, security, health, 
something to do, a .sense of gladness, 
peace of mind, friendships, satisfaction 
in work done, zest. 

Where but in a resident camp can 
these values be found? Compare the 
simplicity of the new experience of pad¬ 
dling a canoe on a glassy lake with that 
of hot-rodding a high-powered car. 
How does one become recognized in a 
high school of 2,000 pupils? How easily 
may this be done in the cabin group 
where each camper is important and 
necessary to the other. Camp can be a 
place where real consistency of values is 
to be found, where all must practice 
the things necessar)^ for the simple life 
which bring a sense of security and con¬ 
fidence. The sense of fatigue that 
comes at the end of a difficult hike, 
the feel of cold water on the body, the 
wannth of sun and exhilaration of a 
wind—such things bring gladness to 
the human mind and soul. 

Friends become real and meaningful 
as we come to depend more and more 
on each other. Co-operation is more 
important than competition in camp, 
satisfaction comes from sei*vice to 
othei's, the moment when campfire 
flames give way to dying embers is one 
of contentment after a full and active 
day. The zest of appetites made keen 
in the open air, the sense of well-being 
that comes after exertion, the exhilara- 


86 


Canadian Camping 






lion of new and challenging experi¬ 
ences—such things strengthen young 
bodies and clear young minds for meet¬ 
ing the problems of life that lie ahead. 

Man was not intended to be an in¬ 
doors animal. Nor is it in his heritage 
to have activity, risk and hard work 
removed from his everyday life. To 
have the satisfaction of accomplishing 
something worth while and meaningful 
to him as an individual is hard to come 
by today. Man must create something 
even if it is the simplest of things. 

Modern society has brought with it 
a number of problems that man’s past 
experience down through history does 
not equip him to solv^e. Where in our 
society do we give our young people an 
opportunity to have these problems dis¬ 
cussed in an intelligent manner? As 
President MacDonald of the University 
of British Columbia has said, “How do 
we prepare these young people for mak¬ 
ing a living and for life? What good 
is a technical education or a profession¬ 
al one if the people we educate have 
not been prepared with the attitudes 
and concepts that will help them face 
some of the problems of living in our 
society?” 

Many say the home should do this. 
Are we as parents prepared and secure 
enough to realize that many of our cer¬ 
tainties must be discarded, concepts 
changed, attitudes modified before we 
can prepare children for tomorrow’s 
world? Dr. Brock Chisholm has said, 
“The children of today must not turn 
out to be like their parents and their 
grandparents. That would be disas¬ 
trous . . . The ability to live harmoni¬ 
ously in a changing total environment is 
a new requirement for today’s citizen. 
To live harmoniously is going to be 
very expensive indeed—in terms of 
some of our loyalties and beliefs, some 
of our comforts and even some of our 
.sovereignty.” 

Can our schools provide the setting 
and climate for open discussion of real 


and controversial issues? Dr. Seeley, 
sociologist at York University, Toronto, 
does not think so when he says “The 
.school’s central function is to tell the 
child the way the world is. All else it 
does with distinction. This it fails to 
do.” Why must we keep from children 
such things as the facts and implica¬ 
tions of sex in our lives, the nature of 
their own natures, the kind of social 
class in which they live, the power of 
big money and big busine.ss? Tlie 
reactionary tone of the recent Royal 
Commissions on Education of the four 
western provinces in wishing to get 
back to the 4-Rs shows little evidence 
of bringing the curriculum to grips 
with today’s problems. 

Are our churches meeting pre.sent- 
day children’s needs by providing a set¬ 
ting where they may question and ana¬ 
lyse, and build concepts in keeping with 
their experience of the world around 

them, or are we clinging to beliefs 
and dogmas of the past? 

I wonder, sometimes, how and where 
in our modern society we are going to 
find the institutions that will provide 
the opportunity for children to be truly 
educated. Then I turn to the resident 
camp where it seems we might have the 
ideal environment for such an educa¬ 
tion. Here are a few obsei'vations that 
may help us to provide a camp pro¬ 
gramme where children could be more 
adequately educated for life. 

1. Camping can be Education in its 
best sense 

What is mean by learning? To learn 
is to live—something lived is something 
learned so it can be recalled when ne- 
ces.sary. Living in the out-of-doors, 

then, can be truly educational. It is 
not hard to recall swimming across a 
mountain lake, paddling a canoe at 
sunset, sleeping in the open under a 
starry sky. Compare the learning and 
what is recalled here with that which is 
often attempted in a formal school¬ 
room’s artificial .setting. Outdoors 


Toronto, Canada, April 1963 


87 ' 


learning leads to equally important ob¬ 
jectives of real education: self-realiza¬ 
tion, enriched living, social maturity. 

2. Camping can provide opportunity 
to experience the concept that co¬ 
operation is perhaps equally impor¬ 
tant to competition. 

In few areas of our lives has there 
been more shallow thinking than in our 
concepts of competition as it relates to 
the life of man. History books sti'css 
the fact that competition is at the heart 
of survival. Danvin perpetuated, 1 
think without intent, the idea that only 
those animal forms that could success¬ 
fully compete with other forms could 
survive. On the other hand, anthro¬ 
pologists and sociologists such as Mar¬ 
garet Mead and Ruth Benedict have 
given us popularly written books point¬ 
ing out that there are societies, even 
today, where no competition exists, and 
they are highly successful in terms of 
living. My plea is this: accept compe¬ 
tition as a part of life, but let us not 
feel that it is the only or even the most 
important part. 

In camp we have an unequalled 
opportunity to let the camper see nature 
in its co-operating mood. Not all 
things in nature are competitive. Birds 
find shelter and food among the bran¬ 
ches of trees; fragile plants are pro¬ 
tected by the shade of larger plants un¬ 
der which they grow. Then, too, can 
we not let children experience the satis¬ 
faction that comes from achievement 
without thought of reward? Do we 
always have to give points or stars or 
awards at camp? Must we have canoe 
races when there is an unexplored lake 
just around the corner? 

3. Camping can improve the child's 
total health and fitness. 

Outdoor recreation can provide pur¬ 
poseful activity to offset the tendency 
to sedentary li\‘ing, where not only 
muscles can benefit but a camper’s 
whole being can be refreshed and stim¬ 
ulated. 


4. Camping can satisfy the child's 
spiritual needs. 

The literature, art and music of most 
cultures is filled with evidence that man 
moves to the out-of-doors to fulfill and 
refresh his inner self. 

5. Camping can bring about a greater 
realization of the democratic way of 
life. 

Origin, material possessions, or social 
level mean little when hiking the long 
trail. Nature is the great leveller: she 
accepts only those who learn to live 
with her. Respect for the simple, yet 
essential skills of wresting a living from 
nature comes to all who combat the 
elements. Then, where better than 
around the camp fire or on an out-trip 
can opportunities be provided for open 
and honest discussion about important 
things? Why not raise the questions 
that come to mind, topics that relate to 
life and values and attitudes, and bring 
out the best in the young, inquiring 
mind? 

6. Camping in small or larger groups 
can greatly enhance social maturity. 

Where else than in group living out¬ 
doors can social development take place 
at such an accelerated rate? All get 
opportunities to develop socially, to be 
responsible, and to share actively in a 
wide variety of conditions which enrich 
experience. 

7. Camping can meet the child's need 
for adventure. 

Man has been relegated to an al¬ 
most inconsequential role in meeting 
his basic needs—food, clothing, and 
shelter. Yet a truly happy person needs 
adventure; and a child, in order to 
develop self-confidence, must have 
“risk” play. Learning to live and be 
skilled in outdoor activities should de¬ 
velop the judgment, the responsibility 
and the ability to participate in ven¬ 
turesome activities without undue risk. 

8. Camping can meet the child's need 
for creativity. 


88 


Canadian Camping 


Many of the anti-social activities 
seen in society today may be partly 
caused by lack of opportunity to create 
with one’s own mind and hands. Our 
schools, by tradition, often frown on the 
child who attempts to be creative or 
different from othei's. Outdoors we can 
create all manner of things: build a 
fire, cook a trout, construct a shelter, 
plant a seed, track a deer; such activi¬ 
ties bring a deep and fundamental sat¬ 
isfaction to us. 

My closing theme is— Camp should 
provide a child with a ^'Child's World'\ 
Let me quote from Robert Hill in the 
American Camping Magazine: “Child¬ 
ren are given little opportunity to run 
the world in which they find them¬ 
selves. If we are anxious to help them 
become able adults interested in, and 
capable of controlling themselves, their 
society and the world, it is important 
we give them opportunities in child¬ 
hood to do just this.” 

We do not give them this chance if 
we impose adult standards on children 
at camp. Certainly direction and firm¬ 
ness are necessary at times, but in camp 
we have the chance to relax somewhat 
from the more formalized standards 
children face at every turn in normal 
life. Let us not be over-meticulous 
about such things as cleanliness. 

Do we not tend to organize our 
camps too much? Children need time 
to “let the spirit catch up on the body”. 
We all become different persons when 
we are alone. Time for loafing, time 
for free choice of activity, time for 
wandering or “just fishin’ ”. Now this 
is quite different from having nothing 
for the children to do. As well as time 
for freedom and choice, we must pro¬ 
vide the climate and atmosphere for 
such opportunities, otherwise free 
choice time may end up in boredom, 
mischief, and even homesickness. 

Might I suggest that the child must 
he involved in the camp. Let him help 


with the planning so that he finds it 
worth while to plan. We can gain in¬ 
sight into his needs too if we let him 
decide what to do. We must listen to 
children: We hardly listen to each 
other any more. We must create the 
environrnent where children are free to 
he original. Children are very flexible; 
let us recognize the importance of being 
able to change our plans. We must 
respect their capacities; we must expect 
failures for we can all learn from them 
too. 

This is a much more difficult ap¬ 
proach than the traditional one of tell¬ 
ing the child what to do. But consider 
how it is that a child learns: — 

Thus a child learns: by wiggling 
skills through his fingers and toes into 
himself; by soaking up habits and at¬ 
titudes of those around him; by pushing 
and pulling his own world. 

Thus a child learns; more through 
trial than error, more through pleasure 
than pain, more through experience 
than suggestion, more through sugges¬ 
tion than direction. 

Thus a child learns: through affec¬ 
tion through love, through patience, 
through undei*standing, through belong¬ 
ing, through doing, through being. 

Day by day the child comes to know 
a little bit of what you know; to think 
a little bit of what you think, to under¬ 
stand your understanding. That which 
you dream and believe and arc, in truth 
becomes the child. 

As you perceive dully or clearly; as 
you think fuzzily or sharply; as you be¬ 
lieve foolishly or wisely; as you dream 
drably or goldenly; as you bear false 
witness or tell the truth—thus a child 
learns. 

THUS A CHILD LEARNS—from the 

First Yearbook, American Associa¬ 
tion for Health, Physical Education 

and Recreation. 


Toronto, Canada, April 1963

ON 

BEING 

A 

LEADER 

Kirk A. Wipper, 
Camp Kandalore 


Being skillful in an activity does not 
necessai'ily mean that you are a good 
activity leader. Developing skills in 
others that will contribute to their hap¬ 
piness and welfare demands under¬ 
standing and experience. 

In the first place, it is important to 
recognize the goal of imparting skills 
at camp. Excellence of performance is 
not the first consideration. Activity 
leadership is concerned with a more 
significant objective, that of contribut¬ 
ing, through the activity, to the growth 
of boys and girls. The activity is the 
medium through which growing camp¬ 
ers find room for expression of latent 
talents, for healthy release of tensions 
and frustrations, for learning about 
themselves and others, for inspiration 
and joy, and generally for progressing 


in the adventure of growing up. A 
sensitivity to this larger purpose of using 
the activity and the learning of skills as 
a tool is really what differentiates acti¬ 
vity leadership from plain instruction, 
where training is the aim. 

It is obvious, therefore, that much is 
demanded of the activity leader. Here 
is an individual who must be sensitive 
to the requirements of the group and 
the individuals in it so that program 
content and method can be adapted 
accordingly. This ability can be ac¬ 
quired through observation, experience, 
study and, of course, a sincere interest 
in the campers. Although this may 
appear to be a formidable task it is not 
without reward. A leader who is able 
to reach the high objective outlined 
above will find a happiness of an abid¬ 
ing nature. He has been instrumental 
in making a significant contribution to 
the camper’s development. 

The target being established, it is 
now fitting to consider ways and means 
of procedure. It will be assumed that 
the leader ha5 taken the opportunity 
to find out about the campers who may 
be coming to him. This may have been 
accomplished by consulting the coun¬ 
sellors, camper files, section heads, or by 
observation of the campers in other 
situations. With this accomplished 
there are generally five steps to pursue. 
These consist of explanation, demon¬ 
stration, execution, correction and re- 
pitition and, finally, recreational appli¬ 
cation. To what may appear to be a 
rigid framework, the instructor brings 
all the flexibility his originality and in¬ 
itiative will allow him. This is the 
activity leader’s duty. 

Explanation involves motivation. The 
leader, through his example and brief 
introductory observations, should in¬ 
spire the interest and attention of his 
group. The reasons for learning the 
particular skill in (juestion should be 
well understood by the camper. Ques- 


90 


Canadian Camping 


lion and response is good teclmique 
here. Members of the group then have 
a stake in things. If no logical purpose 
exists for a skill, perhaps it should be 
deleted. 

In the matter of demonstration the 
leader should have arranged ahead of 
time for a more advanced member of 
the group to do this. This will allow 
the leader to point out important fea¬ 
tures of the skill. Failing this plan the 
leader really has no choice but to per¬ 
form himself. 

The third stage of execution is most 
important. Here is where time should 
be spent using .sensible drill patterns 
which are interesting and enjoyable. 
Everyone, furthermore, should be ac¬ 
tive. The leader must circulate giving 
help where needed, providing encour¬ 
agement and ser\'ing as each situation 
demands. 

The result of careful observation dur¬ 
ing practice will give the leader ideas 
for the correction-repetition stage. It 
is folly to move on without building 
each step thoroughly. A variety of pat¬ 
terns should be used here. Have the 
group, for example, work in pairs so 
that a buddy correction system is at 
work. Invent simple games using a 
particular skill component which re¬ 
quires extra practice. Participating in 
a buddy plan helps a camper to recog¬ 
nize and appreciate the parts of a .skill. 

Recreational activity at the termina¬ 
tion of a period of skill learning is 
sound. It pro\ades a pleasant punctua¬ 
tion point and demonstrates another 
application of the skill in question while 


providing motivation for ensuing peri¬ 
ods. The last impressions of such an 
experience, if happy, will certainly 
colour the tone of those yet to come. 

The succe.ss of each meeting with 
campers in a given skill area is also 
dependent on planning. An outline of 
the general j^rogramme should be made 
and from this, a .series of period out¬ 
lines. Lack of such preparation can 
lead to unhappy consecjuences. Either 
the campers’ experience with an activ¬ 
ity leader will sufl'er from illogical pro¬ 
gression, or serious deletions and repe¬ 
titions may occur, or perhaps the camp¬ 
er will not be exposed to .some of the 
important parts of the activity during 
his term of stay at camp. Adequate 
planning can make appropriate use of 
rainy or very hot days, for which regu¬ 
lar programme would be unrea.sonable 
or undesirable. It is important to plan 
your work and then work your plan. 

To help you judge whether or not 
you are truly a good activity leader the 
following points are suggested. Would 
you think about them and see how you 
“rate”? Remember these are some of 
the rea.sons why an elTective leader is 
so highly regarded and .so e.ssenti^I at 
camp and throughout society. Presi¬ 
dent Smith of Washington and Lee 
University bears out this thought in his 
statement: 

“ .. . then will it be universally recog¬ 
nized that the true leaders and 
makers of the nation are not its mil¬ 
lionaires, not politicians and manu¬ 
facturers, nor railway magnates, but 
those who train and inspire its boys 
and girls ...”

doing it? ▲

The Indian sweat lodge was used for 
cleansing, relaxation and preparation 
lor war. Tiie Indians would prepare 
tlieniselvTs for the sweat lodge by cere¬ 
mony, dancing, chanting and smoking 
the pipe. It was beliexed that switching 
tlie body, combined witli steam, would 
drive the evil spirit from the young 
braves, thus prejjaring them for battle 
or the hunt. 

The constl uction and ir:e of an auth¬ 
entic Indian steam sweat lodge will 
prove an exciting experience for camp¬ 
ers as well as stall'. An igloo-shaped 
sweat lodge 8 feet in lengtli, I feet in 
width and approximately 4 feet in 
height is constructed from green wil¬ 
low' blanches or other saplings. Upon 
completion of the frame the lodge is 
cox ered wdth heavy canx as and made as 
leakproof as possible so that steam may 
be kej)t within the lodge. A large fire 
is built outside the lodge, approximately 
10 feet from one end. Rocks are heated 
(red hot) on the open fire and then 
shoxelled into a screen-covered hole 
located at one end of the lodge. The 
sert'en coxering is essential to prexent 
any splitting rocks from Hying and strik¬ 
ing members in the sxveat lodge. Water 
is then s|)rinkled on tlie rocks causing 
the lodge to fill with steam. \Vhen 
rocks are j)laced in the lodge one must 
be sure that aslies or burning sticks are 
r(*moxed as this causes a strong, pun¬ 
gent odour. 

Folloxving four or fixe minutes of 
steaming, a plunge in the lake or ocean 
]3roxides a stimulating conclusion to 
any programnu*.

• Why We Direct A Camp • 

May and Lome Brown 
Owner-Directors, Camp Deka 


When vvc decided we would open a pri\'ate camp for boys in the historic 
Cariboo of British Columbia in the summer of 1961, we needed, among other 
things, a statement of purpose that would act as a guide-line to our planning 
and operation. 

The folowing statement, therefore, expresses in concise but specific terms why 
we direct a camp. 

WE BELIEVE— 

IT IS THE RIGHTFUL HERIT.AGE OF EVERY BOY TO HAVE 
TFIE OPPORTUNITY OF LIVING WITH EFFICIENCY AND COMFORT 
IN THE OUT-OF-DOORS AWAY FROM THE DISTRACTIONS OF 
CITY ASD URBAN LIFE. 

therefore—we have purposely established Camp Deka on the shores of a 
beautiful inland lake in a wilderness setting. 

THAT CAMPING CAN AND SHOULD BE A TRULY EDUCATIONAL 
GROUP EXPERIENCE. 

therefore—every effort will be made to have boys develop new skills, acquire 
knowledge, learn to live together, and to mature socially. 

THAT BOYS ARE CAPABLE OF TAKING RESPONSIBILITY FOR 
THEIR OWN CONDUCT AND BEHAVIOUR. 

therefore—provision will be made for campers to share in the programme 
planning and in the formulation of camp rules and regulations. 

THAT DESIRABLE ATTITUDES TO BOTH WORK AND PLAY ARE 
ESPECIALLY IMPORTANT TODAY. 

therefore—every boy will be expected to share in camp duties and participate 
in constructive and recreational activities. 

THAT SPIRITUAL GROWTH IS ESSENTIAL TO A WELL-BAL¬ 
ANCED LIFE. 

therefore—ample opportunity will be given for boys to spend quiet periods 
by themselves and with others in the woods, on the water, along 
trails and around the campfire. 


94 


Canadian Camping 






THERE IS AN EVER-INCREASING NEED FOR GREATER INTER¬ 
NATIONAL UNDERSTANDING ON THE PART OF ALL PEOPLES. 

therefore—Camp Deka will be open to boys of any race, color, or creed and 
the programme will include activities international in character; 
the United Nations flag will fly from the camp masthead at 
all times. 

THAT THE CONSERVATION AND WISE USE OF OUR NATURAL 
RESOURCES IS OF MAJOR IMPORTANCE IN TODAY’S SOCIETY. 

therefore—every opportunity will be given for boys to develop a better under¬ 
standing of the inter-relationships of nature, and a knowledge 
and appreciation of the trees, flowers, birds and insects in their 
natural setting. 

THAT THE INDIVIDUAL BOY IS THE MOST IMPORTANT PART 
OF THE CAMP. 

therefore—every part of camp life will be planned to do the most for each 
camper according to his ability, his interests, and his needs. 

THAT TO HAVE FUN IS, IN ITSELF, A WORTHY OBJECTIVE OF 
ANY CAMP PROGRAMME. 

therefore—opportunities will be made for boys to participate in special 
events solely for the laughter and fun of it. 

THAT THE DEVELOPMENT OF LEADERS IS ONE OF THE MOST 
IMPORTANT NEEDS OF OUR WORLD TODAY. 

therefore—through the camp situation and the nature of the responsibilities 
given to counsellors and staff, we can provide a rich opportunity 
to develop the highest forms of leadership. 

THERE IS A DISTINCT NEED FOR A GREATER AWARENESS ON 
THE PART OF PARENTS IN OUR PART OF THE WORLD TO 
SEE THE VALUES OF THE CAMP EXPERIENCE IN THE TOTAL 
GROWTH AND DEVELOPMENT OF BOYS. 

therefore—we hope that through the operation of Camp Deka we will make 
a contribution to the camping movement. 


Perhaps the main reason we are operating this camp is to satisfy ourselves 
that the above statement will work. We believe it will, and are wiling to make 
every eflfort to verify our belief. 

—• 


Toronto, Canada, April 1963

BIBLICAL PAGEANT AT 
CAMP SHALOM, 1962 


Camp Shalom made an excursion 
into ancient history this summer and 
found the experience both rewarding 
and exciting. 

During the first four weeks of the 
camp season, the cabins were assigned 
the names of the Tribes of Israel, and 
in this way acquired all the attributes 
of the Tribes as well—banner, symbols, 
jewel, tribal leaders, all derived from 
the Biblical account. So too, each cabin 
became associated with the particular 
geographic locale in the land of Canaan 
which was the home of its Tribe. 

For four weeks, these latter day 
Tribes of Israel relived the history of 
the Jewish people from the Exodus and 
the wandering in the wilderness to their 
settlement in the land of Canaan, their 
eventual conquest and exile by the 
Romans, and finally the modern return 
of the Jews to Israel. 

About mid-way through the month, 
a pageant was presented as part of the 
Visitors’ Day programme, depicting 
this pilgrimage through history. The 
setting was a natural amphitheatre 
formed by a rise in ground surrounding 
the main sports field. The audience sat 
on the hillside and could look down on 
the pageant, which spread across the 
expanse of the sports field at their feet. 
Behind the sports field could be seen a 
high rock, which served as Mount Sinai 
for the purposes of the pageant. 


The way in which parts of the Bible were 
re-created by Camp Shaloin, 

Ben Zion Shapiro 


Amidst song and dance, recitation 
and dramatic scenes, the story began 
to unfold. Each camper in his own 
tribal group and regalia prepared him¬ 
self at the edge of the field, and then 
at the signal from a Shofar, or cere¬ 
monial trumpet, the massed Tribes ad¬ 
vanced on to the field and occupied 
their positions on a large map of Israel 
outlined on the field. In the centre of 
the field was the stage—a platform sur¬ 
rounded by four poles with brightly 
ribboned decorations used to depict the 
Temple in Jerusalem at the appointed 
time. To the left of the stage were the 
walls of Jericho which were destined to 
fall as a group of campers paraded 
around them with the appropriate fan¬ 
fare and shouting. 

But the high point of the programme 
came when Moses suddenly appeared, 
high on the rock beyond the field, 
bearded and robed, tablets in hand and 
began to intone the text of the Ten 
Commandments. As if to provide the 
most fitting and awesome background 
to these spoken words, Nature conspired 
to heighten this climactic moment. 
Gathering clouds in the Eastern skies 
began to rumble with distant peals of 
thunder and an audible gasp spread 
through the audience. 

Everyone agreed that history had 
truly lived again.

/. D. Scott, 

Camp Wanapitei 


Most people familiar with tripping 
have used a tump-line for can*ying a 
packsack or bed roll, but very few will 
have used one to portage a canoe. The 
practice of using tump-lines on canoes 
is followed at camps on Lake Temag- 
aiiii, almost without exception, and at 
some camps in the province of Quebec. 
This idea for carrying heavy loads 
originated with the Indian tribes of the 
area before the coming of the white 
man and was adopted by the French 
Voyageurs on their long canoe jour¬ 
neys from Montreal to Lake Atha- 
baska. 

The principle involved in tumping a 
canoe is the same as that of using a 
tump on a packsack. That is, to take 
some of the weight off the shoulders 
and to place it on top of the head, or 
directly down the spine. A person can 
support a large weight more easily if 
the load is centred down his spine 
rather than if it is ‘hung’ on his shoul¬ 
ders. For most people the difficulty in 
carrying a canoe is not the weight, but 
rather the control of the large bulk. 
The tump is a help in this regard. 
When going up a hill, the tump, on the 
top of the head, keeps the canoe from 
slipping backwards taking the portage 
thwart off the neck and thereby mak¬ 
ing the canoe somewhat stern-heavy. 
The same is true, to a lesser extent, 
when coming down a hill; there, the 
tump takes most of the weight and 
keeps the portage thwart from digging 
into the back of the neck. 

The rigging of a tump is not diffi¬ 
cult once the canoe has been readied 
for portaging with two paddles lashed 
so that the bases of the shafts or tops 


98 


Canadian Camping 





















()1 ti e blades rest on the thwart and 
tlie tops of tl^c shafts rest on the bow 
seat or bow thwart. The tninps used for 
canoes are much like lliose used for 
packsacks except that the straps at¬ 
tached to the ends of the actual head- 
piece are much longer; a length of four 
feet on each side will suffice. The 
tump is laid across the j^addles so that 
the wide leather head-piece hangs 
down between the paddles. 'The ends 
arc run around the thwart on each 
side betwc'en the jjaddles. and the gun¬ 
wales arc usually in a ‘clove hitch’ so 
that the length between the |)addles 
stays constant. The ends of the tump 
are sc'cured to the gunwale's so that 
there are no loose ends dangling about. 
Now, when the canoe is flijjjx’d foi- 
carrying, the tump will come right over 
the top of the head, d'he length of the 
tump between the paddles should be 
such that when the canoi* is held at a 
conxenient angle for walking, there is 
an even distiibution of weight between 
the paddles on the shoulders and the 
tump on the top of the head. By pull¬ 
ing the canoe down in front, the distri¬ 
bution of w eight is allerc'd lifting the 
canoe completely olT the shoulders. 
Similarly raising the bow jjuts the 
weight back on the shoulders. This, in 
elTect, enables one to take a ivst while 
walking and thereby lengthens the dis¬ 
tance one can portage without a rest. 

At the end of the portage, the tumj) 
is left attach.ed to the canoe and the 
paddles are remoxed as usual. At the 
next portage, the j:)addles are slipjX'd 
back into the lashing on the thwart 
and under the tump and tied in; then, 
all is ready again. 

Almost any form of shoulder-pad 
arrangement can be used in conjunc¬ 
tion xvith a tump and paddles. A 
sxveater or shirt across the sliouldcrs is 
a help. 

Once a jjerson gains some experience 
in using a tumpline on a canoe he xvill 
nexer xvant to portage xvithout one.

CANOE TRIPPING 

A condensation of a Panel Discussion at the O.C,A, Conference, 1962 



Mr. P. G. Gilbert, Camp Nominingue 
Miss Jocelyn Palm, Glen Bernard Camp 
Mr. J. D. Scott, Camp Wanapitei 
Mr. C. R. Blackstock, Carnp Mazinaw 


PGG The trip leader’s primary duty is to gi\'e his campers a few days of enjoy¬ 
ment in the woods, bringing them back happy and healthy. He must have 
a sense of responsibility, considerable skill, lore and fact of the forest, and 
a thorough knowledge of the capacity of his equipment. In reality, the 
success of the trip depends upon liis experience and good judgment more 
than anything else. 

He must plan a trip that will not overburden the campers, presenting to 
them a challenge which he can place within their reach by his conscientious 
preparation and organization. The equipment he chooses, his menu, and 
the nature of the food he takes arc directly related to the basic object in 

tripping. 

The “Gimmick Hunter” on the one hand, bringing with him most of the 
comforts of the city, can ignore the very nature he is supposed to enjoy, 
while the “Imitator of Voyageurs” is fighting nature every stroke of the 
way. Somewhere between these extremes lies a philosophy for each in¬ 
dividual and camp, neither ignoring nature nor fighting it, but making 
use of everything it can offer. 


EQUIPMENT 

IDS What do we ask of a piece of trip equipment? It must be simple and 
foolproof, neither difficult to operate, nor easily broken. Every item must 
have a definite purpose during the trip and be in good shape at the start. 
The canoe, for example, should ha\ e a smooth bottom, taut canvas, strong 
thwarts and seats, and the tumpline securely attached. If campers and 
counsellors learn how to a\ oid scraping it on rocks, and manhandling it on 
])ortages it will still b(' in good shape at the end. 


100 


C.\NADiAN Camping 



Paddles should be strong at the neck of the blade, with a straight grain 
and not split. 

Packs must be large enough to accommodate all the food and equipment. 
Tents should provide enough space to shelter everyone on the trip, and 
there should be enough tarpaulins, (rubber or canvas) to put under 
everyone’s sleeping bag. 

CRB We feel that nature is a pretty good equipper: vve are close to the 
voyageurs really. 

Instead of using tents, we have suggested that our children buy jungle 
hammocks. They take very good care of them. 

JDS Every trip needs a real axe with a good long handle, and each person 
should have a knife of some kind. 

For cooking we use a nesting set of three pots with plates and frying pans 
in the bottom. Sixteen-ounce pannicans can replace the cups and plates. 
A reflector oven or aluminum foil is needed for baking. 

Don’t forget the first aid kit, compas.s, map, matches (in a waterproof 
container), canoe repair kit, scouring pad, file, cord for la.shing, toilet 
paper, a flashlight, two watches, notebook and pencil; and learn how 
to use them all. 

Travel permits arc usually necessary. 

Cameras, maps, and certain kinds of food can be ruined if allowed to get 
wet, and should be protected in cheap plastic bags. 

Bulk foods can be carried in cotton bags. 

CRB Our campers begin their participation in the trip by making their own 
pots from large tin cans. 


CLOTHING 

]P In deciding what clothes to take, consider these factors. Clothing should 
be in good condition, clean, but not new. Each camper should have one 
complete change. Always take raincoats and hats for the inevitable wet 
weather. Rubber and nylon are the best materials. In cold weather a 
wool shirt or heax y .sweater is much warmer than windbreakers or clothing 
made from artificial fibres. 


Q 


What do you think about taking along extra clothing for campers who 
get soaked or leave things at a campsite?

Live With Enthiittiusin ! 

Reprinted from READER'S DIGEST with kind permission of THIS WEEK MAGAZINE 

Youth is not a time of life. It’s a state of mind. It’s a temper of the will, 
a quality of the imagination, a vigor of the emotions, a predominance of courage 
over timidity, of the appetite for adventure over love of ease. 

Nobody grows old by merely living a number of years. People grow old only 
by deserting their ideals. Years wrinkle the skin, but to give up enthusiasm 
wrinkles the soul. 

Worry, doubt, self-distrust, fear and despair — these bow the head and turn 
the growing spirit back to dust. 

Whether 60 or 16, there is in every being’s heart the love of wonder, the 
sweet amazement at the stars and the starlike things and thoughts, the undaunted 
challenge of events, the unfailing childlike appetite for whatnext, and the joy 
of the game of living. 

You are as young as your faith, as old as your doubt; as young as your self- 
confidence, as old as your fear; as young as your hope, as old as your despair. 

So long as your heart receives messages of beauty, cheer, courage, grandeur 
and power from the earth, from man and from the Infinite, .so long are you 
young. 

When the wires are all down, and all the central places of your heart are 
covered with the snows of pessimi.sm and the ice of cynicism, then, and only then, 
are you grown old indeed, and may God have mercy on your soul. 

“Live every day of your life as thought you expect to live forever.” 

Copyright 1962, The Reader's Digest Association (Canada) Limited. Reprinted by permission

LOST AND FOUND 

The Shadow Tip method of 
finding direction. 

J. C. Moore, 

Boy Scouts of Canada, 

Greater Toronto Region 


No one should ever go into the 
woods or a strange country without 
knowing the direction they must take 
to get out. With this knowledge they 
require only a dependable way of find¬ 
ing which direction is north, south, east 
or west. With knowledge of the terrain, 
a compass and knowledge of how to use 
it, one should never become lost. But 
many times we hear “I lost my com¬ 
pass”, or “my compass wasn’t working”. 

The army, air force, Boy Scouts, out¬ 
door organizations and campers have 
been using compasses and a variety of 
other methods to locate direction with 
the stai's and sun. You can pretty well 
depend on the stars at night for direc¬ 
tion. Using simple terms it is easy to 
tell a camper where the Big Dipper is— 
follow the line opposite the handle and 
you’ll find the North Star. .(I’m told 
the degree of error is slight and that it 
will be thousands of years before we 
have to worry in this respect!) 

But much as I hesitate to admit it to 
a camper, the other commonly known 
and used methods of finding direction 
arc subject to considerable error—most 
require time, care, equipment and 
knowledge. When in the bush, doubt 
and panic are all too close at hand, so 
that I have always told campers that 
they can depend on their compasses 
providing the needle is free to turn. 
Unless, however, you know what cor- 


104 


Canadian Camping 














rcction to make for magnetic variation, 
a compass can lead you astray by as 
much as 55° to 90°. 

The common method of using a 
watch and the shadow of a match 
stick—where the hour hand is pointed 
to the sun and halfway between the 
hour hand and 12 o’clock is south is 
dependent on many factors—is the 
watch right? What about daylight sav¬ 
ing time? 

The watch and match stick method 
is based on the assumption that the sun 
moves 15 degrees per hour. In Wash¬ 
ington D.C. in June at mid day the sun 
moves 72 degrees in two hours. Dif¬ 
ferences in latitude, date and time can 
cause error up to 175 degrees. 

There’s the shortest shadow method 
—where a stick is placed in the ground. 
It requires constant watching over a 
period of time and works only at mid 
day. 

The equal shadow method where a 
circle is drawn around the vertical 
stick, requires morning and afternoon 
readings — constant attention to see 
when the shadow intersects the circle 
and then measurements and mathe¬ 
matics. 

The hour method entails marking 
the shadow point in the morning and 
again exactly six hours later, an accu¬ 
rate watch and a great elapse of time. 

If your confidence has now been 
thoroughly shattered don’t panic, for 
there is a new dependable method. 
Bob OwendofT, a 17 year old Boy Scout 
of Falls Church, Va., spent a 4 hour 
period with a group of Scouts-—^I don’t 
want to admit they were lost, but they 
were certainly not sure of direction. 
Bob was familiar with several accepted 
methods of finding direction but some¬ 
thing had gone wrong. 

tnryi to page 107

BanfT, Alberta January’ 23 - 26, 1963

ever held in the West. 

—the first time a Western Executive 
and office have been chosen.

tion has chosen a lady president.

8, Manitoba 4, Saskatchewan 9, British 
from Nova Scotia 1, Quebec 7, Ontario 
Columbia 10, Alberta 62.

sity of Alberta, Edmonton.

Clubs of Calgary.

gary Presbytery, United Church 
Camp Committee.

Boettger, Calgary. 

They have the good wishes of all 
C.C.A. members.

lent, and this included lots of “free 
samples” in eats and drinks.

ranged for a fine array of free gifts and 
literature for all. 

Rufus Good Striker, Blood Indian

and entertainment. 

A square dance with local orchestra’s 
music, a delightful bus tour, superb 
skiing, a grand banquet, stimulating

from page 105 

On his arrival home Bob studied all 
known methods and found them gener¬ 
ally complicated and unreliable. As a 
result of his study Bob has invented a 
method of finding direction that is 
simple, quick, accurate and depend¬ 
able. He calls it the “shadow tip” 
method. It has been acclaimed by 
mathematicians and astronomers. It 
has been enthusiastically accepted by 
the U.S. Army and Air Force after 
50,000 field trials with an average of 
only 8 degree error. 

BOB’S SHADOW TIP METHOD 
Driv^e a stake vertically into the 
ground, allowing a three foot projection 
above the ground level. Mark the tip 
of the shadow on the ground; wait a 
while, ten minutes is sufficient—then 
mark the spot where the tip of the 
shadow is then resting. 

Draw a line between these two points 
—it is always east and west with the 
second point always being east. 

There is rarely a day that it is not 
possible to get a shadow. On a dull 
cloudy day if necessary select a spot 
of ground well out in the open. A 
light sandy or snow covered spot is best. 
It might even be necessary to spread 
a light coloured blanket or even old 
newspaper or other light coloured 
material to get the shadow to show up. 
Then remember— 

—a vertical stick at least three feet 
above ground level. 

—mark the point of the shadow. 

—wait a short interval, 10 minutes is 
enough. 

—mark the spot where the tip of the 
shadow is now resting. 

—draw a line between the two marks 
on the ground. 

—line is always east and west. 

—The second point is always east. 

You can lo.se, break or forget your 
compass or watch; Bob OwendofTs 
“shadow tip” method is simple, quick 
and dependable.

from page 101 

JP I don’t see any point in it. If everyone has a change of clothing and each 
campsite is checked carefully before you leav’e, the problem will not arise. 
Incidentally, it is a good idea to consider the weather forecast when 
deciding what clothes to take. 

SAFETY 

IP Safety, as an attitude, can be brought home to the campers through the 
example set by the staff. Check an unknown area before the campers 
swim there. One alert staff member must remain on shore as a life¬ 
guard. When on the move, keep the canoes relatively close together and 
allow no shifting around in them. These are obvious ways of emphasizing 
safety, but it is just as important to remember safety with regard to your 
equipment too. Judge carefully the load-cariying ability of your campers, 
as well as that of your canoes. It is ver>^ dangerous to overload either of 
them. 

While it is a good idea to carry a minimum of equipment, some things 
must be included for general safety and everyone’s well-being. Protect 
yourselves and the rest of your equipment from sharp objects, by keeping 
axes and knives in strong sheaths; and avoid the danger of broken glass 
by taking food in soft plastic containers instead of glass jars. Always take 
a first aid kit. It need not be elaborate, but should include bandaids, 
sterile gauze, adhesive tape, absorbent cotton, mild antiseptic, burn oint¬ 
ment, aspirin, .scissors, and a needle or two for removing splinters. This 
kit should be completely waterproof. 

0, How do you keep first aid kits readily axailable? 

JDS We put ours on the top of a specially marked pack. 

PGG Our counsellors carry the first aid kit, with the map, compass, matches, and 
many other odds and ends in a small pack. At about fifteen pounds this is 
not a .significant addition to the eighty pounds of canoe they normally 
portage. 

Q Where does first aid stop, and when should you go for help? 

CRB The first aid kit is only a convenience. If any serious illne.s.s or injury 
happens, go for help immediately, particularly if your training and the 
first aid supplies arc not enough to cope with it. 

PREPARATION 

fP Both PG and I take time before the campers go out on a trip to demon¬ 
strate how the equipment is used. Each camper has a chance to see and 
practise a variety of camping skills. This makes them familiar, at least, 
with the processes of pitching a tent, packing, firelighting, and the prep¬ 
aration of certain types of food. 

PGG The demonstration gives the counsellor a chance to estimate the ability 
of his campers. 


108 


Canadian Camping 


CRB Taking them on a one or two meal outing will whet their appetites for 
more and give them the required practice. 

In preparing the children for the trip, we insist that they be able to swim 
50 yards, light a fire in the rain, use an axe, and paddle reasonably well. 
In many camps the trip is regarded as a privilege, and the campers imist 
accept the responsibility of preparing themselves for it. 

Audience: I feel that the basic philosophy which treats canoe tripping 
as a privilege is wrong. Tripping should be the right of every camper. 

CRB I agree, but they must earn that right before they can go. 

PACKING 

PGG In canoe trip packing, a definite quantity of supplies must be distributed 
among a given number of people, forming a single load for each of them, 
if possiblk The loads need not be equal, but should be reasonably 
balanced to the capability of the individual. When using packs exclusively, 
try to .spread food, clothing, and equipment through all of them. Sleeping 
bags and the tent should be folded flat and used in each pack to pad the 
camper’s back. Clothing can fill the corners as the packing proceeds. Staple 
foods in cotton bags should be put on the bottom, followed by tins, 
tightly and carefully placed. At this point the pots might be put in 
one pack, the bread, well cased in caidboard, in another, packages and 
unsealed tins filling the rest. Fold in a tarpaulin, and top it off with a 
raincoat. Remember to keep the lunch .separate from the rest of the food. 
The coun.sellor should keep all the incidental and emergency equipment in 
a small pack under his direct supervision at all times. 

RETURN 

CRB It is the sign of a good camper and a succe.ssful counsellor to bring back 
all equipment in good condition. To complete the trip properly the un¬ 
packing and cleaning .should be planned beforehand. Hang wet clothes on 
a line immediately. Have all injtiries, however slight, and signs of illne.ss 
checked by the doctor. Clean all the equipment and return it to the 
storeroom in an orderly manner. It is a satisfying ending to the trip to 
have everything cleared up and put away efficiently. 

JDS We ask all trips to file a report, for future reference. Its purpose is to 
give information on campsites, portages, rapids and other difficulties that 
might be encountered. 

CRB I'he report is also a chance to rate the campers on their ability, skills, 
and their reaction to the trip. 

PGG An account of the trip, written by the campers themselves, can be very 
interesting to read, as they are usually brutally honest. More important, 
thou!^:h, it gives them a sense of their participation in the trip, and a 
tangible record of where they went and what they did.

MARY & HOWARD GALLOWAY

will Guide You 


Each Christmas season, you hear the 
wonderful story of a Star and how it 
guided the shepherds to Bethlehem 
where Jesus was born. Have you ev^er 
been guided by the stars? 

Walking along a street or across a 
field or through the woods, a sign, a 
gatepost or a tree may serve as a guide. 
But imagine that you are sailing on a 
.ship or flying in an aeroplane high 
above the clouds. Suddenly, you are 
aware that all familiar objects have 
disappeared. 



Not all objects have gone—there is 
the sun still visible. At night, you 
would see many stars. The sun is also 
a star, our most important star, giving 
us light and heat and most useful as a 
guide. 

A ship or an aeroplane is navigated 
by sightings on the sun or a star. 
Sailors and aircrew must fix on these 
objects, then find where they are and 
in which direction they should travel. 
Certain bright stars are sighted on 
more than others in navigation. A 
map of the sky helps you to find the 
star used. 

The winter is our best season for 
studying stars as it gets dark very 
early then and long before bedtime the 
stars appear; in .summer it is very late 


no 


Canadian Camping 




before the stai*s are visible. As you 
view the sky, you will be aware that 
some groups of stars are easier to see 
than others; these are the brightest 
stars in a constellation. A constellation 
is a sub-division of the map of the sky. 

The seven stars in the Big Dipper 
make a familiar outline. Other groups 
of stars form the patterns of a square, 
a triangle, a diamond and a cross. 
These are not as easy for a beginner to 
identify nor as important in finding 
direction. 

Some of the stars in the Big Dipper 
are brighter than others; the two form¬ 
ing part of the bowl are called the 
Pointers, and are almost the brightest. 
If a line is traced through these two 
stars and extended by about five 
times the distance between them, this 
line passes very close to the pole star— 
Polaris. See how easy it is to find Pol¬ 
aris; the pointer stars have guided 
you in finding the direction of North. 

At this time of year, you should try 
to find the square of Pegasus in the 
west and the beautiful constellation 
Orion in the southern sky, with three 
bright stars shining in a central belt. 
The stars will guide you once you 
know a few constellations.

The Case for Camp 
Swimming Classification 
Tests 


Alex Ashenhiirst, 
Camp Pine Crest 


A test is one of the most traumatic 
experiences that we undergo in our pro¬ 
cess of maturation. It can be the source 
of headaches and ulcers. It follows, 
therefore, that any testing programme 
for children should be the result ol a 
carefully considered design. This art¬ 
icle deals with the importance and ])ur- 
pose of camp swimming te.sts for classi¬ 
fication, how they may be designed, 
and the interpretation of their results. 

With a few exceptions, it is essential 
that any camp with a waterfront have 
a specifically designed series of camp 
swimming tests. These tests should be 
carefully graded, simple and succinct. 
This generally rules out Red Cross 
tests, YMCA cards, and other such 
standardized tests. These are carefully 
graded, but their content is far too 
massive for use in classification of swim¬ 
mers. Also a few days are often re¬ 
quired for instruction, and time is 
wa.sted with administrative details. It 
is not advantageous to have all your 
waterfront facilities standing idle while 
potential users arc waiting to be quali¬ 
fied. Some campers may have passed 
adequate tests in previous years, but 
these are often in the minority. Let us 
look a little more closely at the purposes 
of cla.ssification tests and the principles 
upon which they .should be designed. 

These tests benefit both the campers 
and the staff members. It is important 
not to ignore the psychological aspects. 


Many articles have been written about 
the emotions and fears, the needs and 
drives, and the social adjustments 
which confront the delicate emotional 
balance of growing children. Passing a 
test is the goal of the camper and to 
him achievement means recognition 
from his friends and parents. On the 
other hand one cannot make the tests 
too easy or else he will become overly 
confident of his swimming prowess. 
He must be able to appreciate the fact 
that the test was not a “breeze” and in 
this way we hope he will respect the 
water. The importance of passing is 
also reinforced by the additional water¬ 
front ]:)rivileges which are made avail¬ 
able with success. Such .suggestions 
should be kej3t in mind in developing 
the swimming tests. 

Camp swimming tests benefit the 
stall*. The stafT base a good deal of 
their programme on the swimming 
ability of their charges. The counsel¬ 
lors want to know if a boy has the 
.swimming ability safely to go canoeing, 
sailing, or on a canoe trip. The water¬ 
front staff want to know what swim¬ 
ming area a boy can safely handle, or 
whether a boy is in dire need of extra 
swimming le.ssons. These people do 
not want to find this out next week, 
they want to know this the first or 
second day of camp. This indicates 
tests whicli are simple and fast to 
administer. It does not matter whether 
a boy can do fifty yards butterfly, a 
perfect jacknife, or a right-handed re¬ 
verse rolling log. If tests are simple 
the counsellors themselves can do all 
the testing under the direct supervision 
of the waterfront personnel. The efTec- 
tivencss of the regular swimming lessons 
can be determined as the camp swim¬ 
ming tests arc passed throughout the 
season. The waterfront staff announces 
the success of their pupils in the dining 
hall. If, of course, the swimming le.s¬ 
sons are not producing results, steps can 
be taken to intensify and improve the 


112 


Canadian Camping 


lessons before the more formal Red 
Cross and YMCA tests are attempted. 

Camp classification tests help the 
camp director to classify boys when 
they are re-applying for the following 
year. If the campers’ swimming tests 
have been indicated on his application 
form it is a help in arranging harmoni¬ 
ous and homogeneous cabin groups. 

With this background, I will now 
describe the swimming tests at the camp 
with which I am associated. We have 
only four basic swimming tests called 
the A, B, C and D tests. Although the 
naming of them is partly tradition, we 
have kept on with this simplification for 
other reasons. It is much easier to keep 
our records as we can write down “B” 
test, rather than “frog” test or “barra¬ 
cuda” test. It is simpler to tell what 
stage of progression a boy has reached, 
and outsiders can understand this sys¬ 
tem more easily. 

The D test is the first and the easiest 
test. This consists of jumping into deep 
water off a dock, surfacing, and swim¬ 
ming twenty-five feet to a buoy line and 
back. This test serves two purposes. 
Firstly, it is used as an orientation test 
on the first day of camp. Since most of 
the campers arrive by noon, the coun¬ 
sellors make sure that their boys have 
a medical check-up and then they all 
attempt their D test. This enables the 
waterfront staff quickly to assess the 
swimming ability of all the campers, 
carefully note the non-swimmers and 
determine which boys are in immediate 
need of swimming lessons. We may also 
see that a non-swimmer has been in¬ 
advertently put in a cabin of powerful 
swimmers and it may be considered 
wise cjuickly to mo\'e this lad to a more 
suitable cabin group before he is settled 
in. Secondly, this test is a stepping- 
stone which theoretically converts a 
non-swimmer to a swimmer. Although 
this advancement is mainly of a psycho¬ 
logical value, nonetheless, it is of vital 
importance. Throughout the camp. 


recognition is made of such an achieve¬ 
ment and it evokes a considerable 
amount of satisfaction in the camper. 

Most people can vividly remember 
the first time they swam in deep water 
and we feel that it creates an attitude 
of respect for deep water. Our camper 
now knows that he is progressing and 
his next goal is his C test. 

Tlie C test consists of jumping into 
deep water, swimming twenty-five yards 
on your front and then twenty-five 
yards on your back. Like the D test, 
the privileges gained are rather super¬ 
ficial because one cannot say that a C 
tester is a good swimmer. One reason 
for including the swimming on the back 
is subtly to discourage overconfident 
D testers from wanting to advance too 
quickly until they have had more swim¬ 
ming lessons. Back sculling is much 
easier to do than the crawl and a 
camper at this stage should have at 
least one resting stroke. 

The B test is the first indication that 
a swimmer has .some degree of skill. 
To pass it, a camper must swim a dis¬ 
tance of 220 yards across an open bay 
accompanied by a boat and two staff. 
Any stroke is permitted unless it is 
really pathetic. Since the bay is quite 
deep and the swimmer is a considerable 
distance from shore we feel this test 
is much more valuable than swimming 
this distance in a pool. With success, 
the camper’s privileges are vastly in¬ 
creased. A camper with a B test is 
allowed to go out in .sailboats, canoes 
and in certain circumstances he may 
go on a short canoe trip. 

Jump into deep water wearing py¬ 
jamas and high laced running shoes, 
remove this clothing in the water, tread 
water thirty seconds with hands out of 
water, .swim one quarter mile acro.ss 
an open stretch of water, and a camp¬ 
er has pas.sed his A test. If one lias 
never attempted to swim with clothes

on, one cannot easily appreciate the 
difficulty of trying to stay afloat in such 
a situation. This is the feeling that the 
camper should experience since most 
boating mishaps will occur when jieople 
are fully clothed. The removal of 
clothes is more of an exercise than any¬ 
thing else .since the swimmer should 
hold on to his boat or canoe. However, 
it could jnove u.seful. If an individual 
is able to carry out these stejxs including 
the feet-only treading water, this person 
has learned how to relax and conserve 
his strength in the water. Relaxation 
is the ultimate aim for proficient swim¬ 
ming and it is felt that an A tester is 
approaching this objective. To sub¬ 
stantiate this, over the past five years 
not one instance has been recorded at 
our camp where a boy failed the .swim¬ 
ming part of the test after passing the 
first part. Believing that this test serves 
its purpose, “A Testers” are allowed to 
go on canoe trips, they may try higher 
canoeing tests and may participate in 
virtually any waterfront activity. Pur- 
po.scly, this test is .somewhat overde¬ 
signed. An occasion where a boy would 
have to swim one quarter of a mile 
would be very rare, but one is really 
a.ssured that such a boy could swim a 
few feet to his overturned canoe and 
hold on for a while until help arrived. 

These are our camp swimming tests. 
Again, it must be emphasized that they 
are designed for a waterfront orientated 
camp, with an age range of eight to 
fourteen years. Not all camps could 
use them. Some camps could u.se no 
part of them at all, while camps which 
cater to a younger age grouj) would 
probably modify them. 

As a prerequisite to organizing and 
maintaining a safe and progressiv’e 
.swimming programme, it .seems abso¬ 
lutely essential to hav e camp swimming 
cla.s.sification tests. The essence of their 
efi'ectivene.ss is their simplicity and this 
is the fundamental criterion upon 
which they should be designed.

not, there is an aura that hangs about 
us, generated by the status of our posi¬ 
tion. From this special position we can 
touch many young people, campers and 
counsellors, so that their lives may be 
richer and fuller because they have 
known us. 

In a world that is fairly barren of 
guiding lights, we could help uncertain 
youth over the moral shoals they are 
encountering. In a world that needs 
people who can listen to, talk to, and 
by e.xamplc influence the lives of young 
people positively, we are really derelict 
in our responsibilities as camp directors 
when we pass along these most import¬ 
ant functions to other and usually 
younger and less experienced staff 
members.

so many assistants between us and the 
campers, let’s hire them to back us up.

BOOK REVIEWS 



RAINY DAY FUN FOR KIDS by 

Claire Cox; Association Press (in 

Canada, G. R. Welcli Co., Toronto) 
1962. $4.30. 

When it rains and rains, and the cry 
goes up, “What shall we do now?” 
what do you do? Quite often there is 
an assortment of materials at hand, and 
when you lay them out invitingly in a 
suitable space, children’s creativity takes 
takes over or can be launched with 
some ingenious suggestions by an inter¬ 
ested adult. 

However, both children and adults 
can run out of ideas when faced with 
a long session of rain. In this book 
Claire Cox describes 505 games, tricks, 
things to make, quizzes and skits. She 
arranges them alphabetically in Chap¬ 
ter 5. Out of all this how do you find 
what you want? Her approach is this: 
she devotes Chaptei* 2 to Which of 
These Situations is Nearest Yours? 
Each situation is followed by an alpha¬ 
betic list of appropriate activities to be 
found in Chapter 5. A few situations 
seen at random are: Is the Picnic, Hike 
or Cookout Rained Out?, Do You 
Want to Make Silly Creatures?, Will a 
Few Stunts and Challenges Make Your 
Group Forget the Rain? 

Chapter 3 goes into What\s' on Hand? 
The author lists a variety of materials 
and under each suggests suitable activi¬ 
ties from Chapter 5. While she does 
include clay, cones, pebbles, sand, fea¬ 
thers and seeds, most materials are not 
indigenous to camps and would have 
to be obtained beforehand. Chapter 4, 
Where You Can Find What You Need, 
includes friends, magazines and news¬ 
papers, neighbourhood and local busi- 


ne.sscs, pamphlets, and she indicates 
where you could write for many speci¬ 
fic materials. Although some “scroung¬ 
ing” at camp could be rewarding, most 
of the sources would need to be tapped 
in advance. 

While some of us would probably 
prefer to have resource books of acti¬ 
vities organized so that we find craft 
ideas in one chapter, table games in 
another, party preparations and favoui*s 
in another, and so on, this would be a 
helpful book if you could start from 
your situation or what materials you 
had available at the moment. The sug¬ 
gested activities range from preschool 
level to teenager in the hope of assist¬ 
ing any recreation worker who.se out¬ 
door programme is “rained out”. 

D.M.D. 


THE LONELY LAND by Sigurd F. 

Olson; Alfred A. Knopf (In Canada, 

McClelland and Stewart, Toronto 
16), 1961. $4.95. 

A dramatic account of a thrilling 
canoe trip down 500 miles of the 
Churchill River by a group of six men, 
fired with the romance of the old voy- 
ageur life. Inhere arc vast stretches of 
country across the Canadian Shield 
where rivers and lakes are still as wild 
and beautiful as when the brigades of 
fur-traders made their annual journeys 
to exchange trade goods for furs from 
the Northwest. Such is the setting for 
this trip from He a la Crosse in Saskat¬ 
chewan to Cumberland Floiise on the 
Manitoba border. 

Each of the men had a unique con¬ 
tribution to make to the venture, in 
skill and interests, even though—with 


I 16 


Canadian Camping 






one exception—their professions were 
business or diplomatic. The exception 
was the author, one of the best-known 
living woodsmen of the continent, call¬ 
ed by his party ''Bourgeois'', title of the 
voyageur brigade leader. Journals of 
the early explorers of the route they 
travelled were carried by Eric Morse, 
Executive Director of the Associated 
Clubs of Canada, who would read 
aloud by the campfire at night. 

At every chapter heading Frances 
Lee Jacques has sketched the scene in 
an exquisite pen-and-ink drawing, and 
this is followed by a quotation from the 
diary or journal of one of those intre¬ 
pid explorers who knew this route— 
Alexander Mackenzie, George Simp- 
.son, David Thompson, Alexander 
Henry, etc. I'he shooting of white 
water rapids, the routines of canoe-trip 
life are delightfully outlined, and would 
fire both counsellors and senior campers 
with enthusiasm for that most stimulat¬ 
ing of all camping experiences, the 
canoe trip. 

As Olson puts it, “If a man can pack 
a heavy load across a portage, if he can 
do whatever he has to do without com¬ 
plaint and with good humour ... if he 
can somehow keep alive a spark of 
adventure and romance as the old-time 
voyageurs seem to have done, then any 
expedition becomes more than a jour¬ 
ney through wild country. It becomes 
a shining challenge and an adventure 
of the spirit.” 

D.M.D. 

Editor's Note —When Mr. Eric Morse 
addressed a meeting of Hunters and 
Anglers in Toronto January 28th this 
year, Mr. Jack Ridley, Chairman of the 
Quetico Foundation, introduced him as 
a keen historian and authority on the 
life and travels of the early explorers 
and voyageurs of Canada. The speech 


that followed was full of fascinating 
information. Any camp group would 
be fortunate to hear him or to see his 
pictures of such canoe trips as this one 
through llie Lonely Land. 

A COOL CURVING WORLD, by R. 

B. Miller; Longmans Canada Ltd.; 
1962; $5.25. 

A book for your camp library. Coun- 
.sellors and older campers will enjoy 
reading it. Parts would be excellent for 
reading aloud around a campfire on a 
canoe trip. 

Dr. Miller is a biologist, whose .scien¬ 
tific interest is fish and “other creatures 
which live with them or on them.” His 
outdoor laboratory includes Algonquin 
Park, Lesser Slave Lake, Great Bear 
Lake and George Lake in the eastern 
Rockies. He describes his adventures of 
travelling through the wilderness, hu¬ 
man and animal encounters, camping 
practices born of necessity. He also 
tells us a great deal about fish life and 
problems of conservation, disease and 
gON'ernmental eflorts to preserve water¬ 
ways and water life. 

Dick Miller’s humour and his com¬ 
ments on how to live properly and com¬ 
fortably in the outdoors will be of 
special interest to camp people. He de¬ 
scribes a young man who had read too 
much of wood lore and insisted that 
living outdoors meant roughing it for 
roughing it’s sake. Whereas, “genuine 
dwellers in the woods, men like trap¬ 
pers, timbercruisers, rangers . . . try to 
manage to be as comfortable in the 
woods as they would be if they had 
stayed at home. Only enthusiastic ama¬ 
teurs feel that if you are being com¬ 
fortable, you are being sissy.” 

M.L.N.

KAMP KaPERS 

She was very young, very pretty, and 
\'ery much in love. She just couldn’t 
help telling the other counsellors about 
him. He was special, unique, and hers. 
She had a ring to prove it. Nothing 
like this had ever happened before. 
The counsellors were tolerant, up to a 
point. However, there is a limit. Then 
someone had the bright idea. She was 
scheduled to do the flag-raising on 
Thursday morning. If they made a few 
preparations. . . 

Wednesday evening the flag was re¬ 
moved from its place, unfolded, re¬ 
folded and returned. Half-a-dozen 
counsellors, all giggling, went their v^ari- 
ous ways. It was a wonderful scheme. 
But, next morning she had a headache 
—a real one. So, it was the director 
who took flag-raising. Six counsellors 
gasped; then stood rigidly at attention, 
their faces dead-pan. The three juniors 
in the colour party marched forward, 
in solemn dignity and out of step. They 
came to a halt; the centre one gave 
the flag a yank, and it broke open. 
Tiny particles of coloured paper in a 
shower came gently down onto the 
heads of the three small and mystified 
campers, and the not-so-much mystified 
director. (There must have been two 
whole packages of confetti in that flag 
—some of it lay all summer beneath the 
flag-pole!) O well, it might have been 
the egg which found its way into a flag 
at another camp! —•
